cues.text: On Holy Thursday, 1643, in the French village of Pressac, the parish priest celebrated Mass and distributed Communion to the assembled faithful as usual.

Afterward, following custom, he placed the chalice — which still held a consecrated Host — back in its repository near an altar dedicated to the Blessed Virgin, and the townspeople returned to their ordinary work for the day.
Candles left burning near the altar sparked a fire that spread quickly through the surrounding woodwork before anyone noticed.
Parishioners rushed back to the church in alarm once the flames were discovered.
By the time the fire was brought under control, the chalice itself had been completely consumed.
It was reduced, along with much of the altar area, to ash and melted metal.
A Host Beneath a Tin Bubble
Searching through the wreckage afterward, those clearing the site found that only the foot of the chalice had survived the heat at all.
A small bubble of tin had formed beneath it during the fire, sealing within it the consecrated Host.
When the bubble was opened, the Host was found completely intact and undamaged.

The Host recovered from beneath the melted metal was consumed the following day, in keeping with ordinary practice for a consecrated Host too small a quantity to preserve indefinitely as a standing relic.
What survived instead was the documentary record of the event and, notably, a set of stained-glass windows in the church of Pressac depicting the different stages of the fire and its aftermath.

The Pressac account belongs to the same broad family as Bagno di Romagna, Faverney, and several other fire-related Eucharistic traditions from this period — a consecrated Host surviving heat that destroyed the vessel meant to protect it.
Centuries after the Host itself was consumed, the windows of Pressac preserve not a relic but a record.
They show, in colored glass, a fire that took everything around the altar except the one thing the parish most needed to remain.
